name: Libya
system_note: Rival governments in Tripoli and the east.
snapshot: Split between rival governments since 2014, Libya saw fighting shut its biggest refinery in 2026 before the two sides agreed to hold elections within two years.
culture: Libya's coast holds some of the best-preserved Roman cities anywhere, at Leptis Magna and Sabratha, though war has kept tourists away. Tribal and family ties are central to identity and politics. Amazigh, Tebu and Tuareg minorities have revived their languages and culture since 2011 after decades of suppression under Gaddafi.
society: Africa's largest proven oil reserves fund public salaries and subsidies for most Libyans, but militias, rival central bank claims and blockades disrupt income. Libya is a main departure point for migrants crossing to Italy, many held in abusive detention centres. Floods in Derna in 2023 killed thousands after dams burst.
situation: Fifteen years after Muammar Gaddafi was killed in a drainage pipe, Libya still has two governments, two parliaments and, in practice, two armies, sitting on Africa's largest oil reserves. The internationally recognised government in Tripoli under Abdul Hamid Dbeibah controls the west. The east and south answer to the 82-year-old field marshal Khalifa Haftar and a rival cabinet under Osama Hamad. The 2021 elections that were meant to end this were cancelled days before polling, and both camps have found the division comfortable.

2026 showed the cost. On 8 May, fighting with heavy weapons between Tripoli-aligned security forces and local militias forced Libya's largest refinery, at Zawiya, to shut, with shells landing in civilian neighbourhoods (Security Council Report). Drone strikes later hit refinery facilities, and parts of the country suffered fuel and power shortages despite sitting on all that oil. Then, on 30 August, after months of UN-led talks, the rival sides signed an agreement in Tripoli to hold national elections within two years, which the Security Council called an important step (Africanews). Libyans have heard promises like this before. The question is whether the men who benefit from the split will let a vote remove them.
power: No single authority. The UN-recognised Government of National Unity and a Presidential Council govern from Tripoli; the eastern House of Representatives backs a rival Government of National Stability and Haftar's Libyan National Army. Armed groups hold real power on the ground in both halves.
holders: Prime Minister Abdul Hamid Dbeibah in Tripoli; Field Marshal Khalifa Haftar in the east.

update.html: On 22 November sea drones sank a Russian warship docked at Benghazi's naval base and struck a merchant ship offshore; Ukraine claimed the attacks, and the UN mission called for an independent investigation and warned that Libya must not become a battleground for foreign conflicts. The eastern-based House of Representatives then proposed a joint committee with Tripoli's High State Council to unify state institutions and prepare elections, and Khalifa Haftar visited Turkey at President Erdogan's invitation on 24 November, a sign of how far Ankara and Benghazi have come since the 2019 to 2020 war.

story: Italy seized Libya from the Ottomans in 1911 and crushed resistance brutally. After World War Two it became a kingdom under King Idris, and oil was found in 1959. Muammar Gaddafi overthrew the king in 1969 and ruled for 42 years. The 2011 uprising, backed by NATO airstrikes, killed him, and the country split between rival governments and militias in the west and the east, where Khalifa Haftar rules.
